utterances.text: So what sort of contribution did Crni and Mr. Todorovic provide to the domestic problems that faced the municipality? Did they discuss the water supply for instance or medical aid or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't talk about those topics, those were the least discussed topics. Djordjevic spoke about the military. Crni about his -- what were they called, sareni. Todorovic talked about arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following this meeting, did you report to your commanders, Mr. Antic and Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric of the events at the Crisis Staff? Did you debrief them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Radovan Antic what had been discussed there. And I said to him I didn't want to attend any more meetings of the Crisis Staff, and I said that something should be done in a way so that I wouldn't have to go there again, because I saw that I wasn't really wanted there and I felt humiliated, not by everyone but I heard expressions such as Turks, balija, and that hurt me, and Crni and Stiv always said those words, and then the detention of people just because they bore a different name or had a different religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- you had to make moves, did you, to make sure that you didn't remain on the Crisis Staff? Namely by speaking to Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was Antic who helped me. What helped me was simply the fact that I was a Muslim and that I wasn't wanted there, but I say again it wasn't everyone who found me undesirable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the years since April of 1992, have you ever found out why it was that the Crisis Staff invited you there if they didn't want you there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know who nominated me. Perhaps -- I say perhaps -- Blagoje Simic didn't mind my presence. He knew me well. But Stiv, Bozo Ninkovic, Simeon Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not want me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just move to another topic, if we can. The transfer of the prisoners to Brcko. All of those men who were held in the TO and who were transferred to Brcko were men who had been arrested by these paramilitaries and Todorovic's Serbian police, correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrests were mostly carried out by Stevan Todorovic's police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But -- fine, but all of them, all of them, had been arrested either by Todorovic's police or by the paramilitaries, the Serbian paramilitaries? Not one of them was arrested by the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that the members of the 4th Detachment, and I can swear to this on my children, that not a single member of the 4th Detachment arrested a single Muslim or Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor were they authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And so therefore you must agree that they were not prisoners who had been captured in fighting with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so therefore you must agree with me that they were not prisoners who had been captured in fighting with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA didn't fight that morning at all, nor did the 4th Detachment engage in combat on that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric ever explain to you why the JNA was taking these men into its custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He just said JNA never arrested anyone and now the question was did Mr. Zaric explain why the JNA was make taking these men into custody? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll provide the foundation. I'll go on and do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men were transferred from Brcko, sorry, from Bosanski Samac, to Brcko, and it was Mr. Zaric and the JNA that brought about the transfer, correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions in which these imprisoned Muslims were living were impossible. There were murders, beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sorry, Mr. Topcagic, but we must move on. I know all about the bad conditions. It's a really simple question, okay? It was Mr. Zaric and the JNA that carried out the transfer from Bosanski Samac to Brcko, that is plain as day, correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to help these people and they did that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about their motives, I'm just asking you a very simple question. It was the JNA, officers of the JNA, who brought about the transfer from Bosanski Samac to Brcko, wasn't it? It was a fellow called Commander Nikolic and Momcilo Petrovic and Mr. Zaric himself, of course.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They organised the transfer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. And then when they arrived at Brcko, they were put into a JNA garrison, into a JNA prison?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't in prison. They were in rooms used by the army before. It was not a prison. And the conditions were normal. They had water, toilets, beds, everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they couldn't leave, could they? They couldn't go home, take a walk down the street could they? They were in custody and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were detained, but in far better conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in greater security n Brcko, in comparison with Samac. Nobody beat them, mistreated them, they had everything that they were supposed to have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hear what you say, thank you. So can you tell the Trial Chamber why it is that the JNA took these men into its custody?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They managed to get these people out of the TO, which was a place of death, of sexual assault, a dungeon, a black dungeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Topcagic, I understand and I hear what you've got to say. I understand that you're trying to convey the meaning that this was a humanitarian gesture conducted by Mr. Zaric [Realtime transcript read in error "Czar"] and his associates. I understand that. And if I want to ask you about that, I'll ask you about that. Okay? But I'm not asking you about that. Please, listen to the question, we will finish this quickly, okay? All I'm asking you is this: These men were not captured in JNA -- in fighting with the JNA. These men were prisoners of the Serbian police and the paramilitaries. Yet they were placed in the custody of the JNA. Now, do you know why the JNA took custody of these men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For humane reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May we have just one small correction for the transcript? Again, this appeared for the second time, on page 47, line 10, when referring to Mr. Zaric it says Mr. Czar, so just that small correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, I'm grateful to Mr. Lazarevic for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And maybe I'll just like to ask what will be the time limit for the cross-examination because we had allotted two and a half hours and now it's been more than two hours and 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me actually because the cross-examination started yesterday. MR. DI FAZIO: I know that. Your Honours, according to my case manager who is watching I'm just past the end of my allotted time. I really only got two areas left. I think I could probably wrap it up in about 15 minutes, if you allow me. There is just two topics really. Might I say that I've already skipped a lot of what I had intended. Just two areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because two and a half hours was sufficient Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. No more than 15 minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, I appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one other, two other topics, first of all at Brcko, you -- at Brcko, you spoke to Osman Jasarevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You proposed to him that he join the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me for assistance and I said to him, because we were related, I said, "Osman, I can only help you if you -- when you join the 4th Detachment. What matters is that you get out of here. And then we'll find a solution and see what we can do further."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were being honest with him? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell the Trial Chamber how it is, and why it is, that Osman Jasarevic could leave the custody of the JNA if he joined the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a very small possibility. Perhaps in that way, I could get him out of prison. Nobody imposed those conditions on them. But through some people, I could perhaps ask for this to be settled. Maybe he wouldn't even have taken up a weapon, although he's related to me I have to say he was one of the most extreme Muslims in Samac. He was an extremist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was more than -- your position is, isn't it, that it was more than a small chance? Isn't your position that you were sure that if you did so, he would be released from detention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have the answer to this he said, the witness, on page 49, line 5, he said yes, well it was a very small possibility and now the Prosecution is trying to put him that it was more than a small chance. This is not what the witness stated. MR. DI FAZIO: All right, perhaps the way my question was framed didn't come across -- my meaning didn't come across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and also, if the Prosecution wants to challenge the witness, they can do so. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Topcagic, that your position is that you told him that you could help him if he joined the 4th Detachment and that you were sure that if he did so, he would be released from detention?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to him that he should say he was going to join the 4th Detachment and whether he would actually take up a rifle or not we would see that later but that's what I said to him, that we could try to solve the problem in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever informed anyone, when talking of this topic, that you were sure that he could be released from detention if he joined the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that to him, although I myself wasn't sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you told anyone else in recent times, in discussing this topic of Jasarevic, that you said to Mr. Jasarevic that you were sure that if he joined the 4th Detachment, he would be released from detention?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've asked me this three or four times and I always gave you the same answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. What made you think that there was some chance that he would be released if he joined the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to be quite sincere now. I helped his whole family, his mother, his three sisters, his cousins, his mother and his sister asked me to help him. His brother was also in prison. His mother and his sister begged me to help him if I could, in any way, and I looked for a way to help him, and this whole family left for Serbia. They stayed with me for a month [as interpreted], and from there they went on to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topcagic. And I'm sure that the Prosecution agrees with you that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, one clarification for the transcript. This is not actually what the witness said they stay with me for a month, because what he actually said is they stayed with my family for a time because he wasn't obviously in Serbia. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Of course, I'm sure Mr. Lazarevic is correct and I accept what he says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Topcagic, all I'm asking you is this: Not about how the Jasarevic family felt, I think we all know. What I'm asking you is this: What made you think that there was some chance that he would be released if he joined the 4th Detachment? How did you think it might work? How did you think that might spring him from jail or from custody?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for any way out, for any chance to get him out. I wasn't sure it would succeed. I didn't discuss it with anyone. I didn't consult anyone. I simply wanted to make the situation easier for him. I wanted to try to help him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On this occasion at Brcko, was Colonel Nikolic present? Colonel Nikolic of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Nikolic being there, because his headquarters was in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just answer yes or no and we'll finish quickly. Do you know if there was a gentleman named Lazo Trojan who was present?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Lazo and I arrived at Brcko together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you spoke to Jasarevic, was that in an interview room in which you, Mr. Zaric and Trojan and Colonel Nikolic were present?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The witness has just said that Mr. Nikolic wasn't there. MR. DI FAZIO: Fair enough, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a room when all of those people except for Mr. Nikolic was present?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I didn't see Simo Zaric until he set out for Brcko, so I didn't see Simo Zaric or his driver. It was Lazar Stanisic called Ziga and I, and Jasarevic happened to be outside with a policeman, I don't know why, whether he had gone to bring some water or something but I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Topcagic, just please if you can answer me yes or no to the following questions. Were you present at the exchange in Sid in early July, 1992? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were held there for about two days, held up for about two days because of some problem, so you arrived on the 4th, the exchange happened on the 5th, correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But over two days --

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know we spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. During that time, Zaric, Mr. Zaric was present and Mr. Miroslav Tadic were present, correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man -- one of the people organising the exchange was Mr. Tadic, correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velimir Maslic and Svetozar Vasovic worked on the exchanges. As far as I know, the decisions were all made by Stiv, as to who could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, is that Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so he -- correct, yes or no, tell me, Todorovic was the man mainly responsible for picking who was going on exchanges and who wasn't?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was he who decided who would be exchanged and who would remain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. Now, you and Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic all saw the people being exchanged on the 5th, the day that they actually went across the line?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I can't remember the date but I did see that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the people who were being exchanged out of Bosanski Samac, that is the people who were leaving Bosanski Samac to cross the Croatian lines into Croatian-held territory, had no choice but to leave Samac? In other words, it wasn't voluntary?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They volunteered at the Red Cross, in terms of who wanted to go and be exchanged, and when people would come to the line, then they would be asked, over there, the line, do you want to go back? Or do you want to go across? If you want to go back, you can return to Bosanski Samac again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying they had a choice?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have a choice. And there were cases of people going back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your view, would you describe what you saw on the 5th of July as a great human tragedy, this exchange?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two buses. Well, there were men, women, children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just casting your mind back, thinking about the whole event in its entirety, what you saw, not a detailed analysis, just thinking back about it, in your view, is what you saw a great -- would you describe it as a great human tragedy?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, that was a tragedy. Everybody who has to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several reasons why these people left their homes. Would you let me finish? Would you let me finish what I started to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Defence counsel will clarify anything that needs to be clarified, and they will have that opportunity after I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the extra time is over, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please I've just got --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please I've got about six or seven more questions on another topic that I really need to put. It's a matter of minutes, not even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, it will be impossible to control the time because you should have timed yourself when you were preparing your questions. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I realise that, if Your Honours please. I just seek this indulgence on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ten minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you and I probably won't even need that, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to move now to a completely different topic, Mr. Topcagic. Have you ever contacted any witnesses in this case, Defence or Prosecution, in relation to their proposed testimony?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question? I just want to ask you one more thing. When I am responding, please don't interrupt me. And repeat this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Rest assured, Defence counsel will clarify anything that I left obscure. Now, my question is: Have you ever contacted any witnesses in this case, Defence or Prosecution, in relation to their proposed testimony?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. Could you put it a bit slower? I don't know which witnesses this refers to. Does it refer to witnesses who are testifying against Mr. Zaric, Blagoje Simic and Miroslav Tadic? Or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. It refers to all -- any witnesses for any defendant or any Prosecution witnesses. Have you ever contacted any witnesses of whatever description, witnesses for this case, in relation to their proposed testimony?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the testimony of Salkic, Ibrahim Salkic, nicknamed Ibela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the contact?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to my home, with his wife, with his daughter, and he started crying, and he said, Fadil, I had to lie over there in court, because the AID service of Bosnia-Herzegovina worked on me. I didn't even want him to enter my house because I knew of the lies that he had told here in this courtroom. I went with him, with him, to a joint friend and that is where we continued this conversation. When we talked about all of this, he took the telephone and he even called up this man who works in this service, the AID, he wanted me to talk to him, and I refused. Until the present day, he's been coming to my home and we are good pals. Another encounter that I had with a witness was with [redacted]is his nickname. Now, what's his name? His nickname is [redacted]. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that I think Mr. Lazarevic is warning us that these -- this portion of evidence should be redacted, and kept out of the transcript because these are protected witnesses so I'd ask that that immediately be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only the second one. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, only the second one, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the testimony of [redacted], I don't know his --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just hold it there. If Your Honours please it might be wise if we move into closed session at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that he resorted to blatant lies?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now no open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he resorted to blatant lies you're talking about blatant lies told her in this Chamber, to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise Your Honour and to my friend in order to avoid misunderstanding because we were partly in private session and now we are in open, when you said he, could you make a reference of who you are thinking? Please. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes, okay. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that Alija Fitozovic resorted to blatant lies, you're talking about blatant lies told here in this Court, in this Tribunal, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow the testimony of the witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it would be on television, and also it would be on the BH programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When this trial started, well over a year and a half ago, you expected to be a witness in this case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't expect it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first find out that you might be a witness in the case?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wished to be a witness, that's what I wished, because when I heard all the things that were being said and what was going on, I wanted to come here and to look everyone straight in the eye and to say what I had to say. Especially I wanted to face some of my Muslims because I am ashamed of some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And did you then volunteer your services as a witness?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when, having done that, did it become clear to you that you would be indeed a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know until a few days ago, a few days before I came here. I gave a statement but I didn't know that I would be a witness. I gave a statement that I would respond to any summons by this Court. This was in December, I think. I can't remember exactly, when your people came, when your investigators came. I gave my word that I would appear in court and I'm glad that I came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks, and since December at least have you been following the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was interested in this, all the time. Not only from our parts. I was also interested in what's going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, have you ever offered any witnesses any reward or advantage, financial or otherwise, in order for them to testify or in order for them not to testify?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any financial resources for my own living. I don't work. My wife doesn't work. I don't have any money. I live in my mother's house. I have my own house which I never managed to finish. I started building it before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it your answer is no, you've never made such offers?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm offering something for the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not offer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your position, Mr. Topcagic. You're saying no, no, you've never done it and you would never do it. I understand your position. Now I just want to ask you this: Are you aware of any Defence witnesses being offered payment or given payment in addition to the sort of -- the legitimate expenses that are paid by the Tribunal to witnesses?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't believe that. Certainly, at least as far as our lawyers are concerned, at least what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever told or informed any Defence witnesses that when they come to the Tribunal, they should blame everything on Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that to anyone, but I wish -- I wish you'd give me sometime, a bit of time, if you can, so that I could say something, because many people here did not say what they were supposed to say, as far as he's concerned. Could you please allow me to say that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, if Your Honours please I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic? You want to ask some questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Topcagic, good afternoon. I am Igor Pantelic, attorney at law, Defence counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic. Since the Prosecutor put some questions to you during the cross-examination, some questions that have to do with my client and your answers also had to did with my client at last partly so I'm going to put a few questions to you by way of clarification, nothing more than that. A short while ago, you were saying to the Prosecutor things about some witnesses who had certain experiences and who told you about certain things and you mentioned the AID service. Is this a news agency? Is this a cultural and arts society? What is this, for the sake of the transcript. Let's know what it is.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a secret intelligence service of the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to the Prosecutor's questions, that had to do with that first meeting where this alleged Crisis Staff was, you mentioned my client, Dr. Blagoje Simic, in the context of him having known you well and you having known him well. Please tell me, what is the attitude of Blagoje Simic to you? Is it an attitude of respect, or is his manner to you very cold? Could you just explain this for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Trial Chamber -- as far as Blagoje Simic is concerned, I have to say that he was correct to me and I have to tell you about one more thing. He probably remembers this particular event. When I came to complain about Stevan Todorovic, that's when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what was falling on Samac.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Simic I'm sure you remember this, you offered me a drink. You listened to me, because I had terrible problems with Stevan Todorovic. You said to me quite literally and that's the way I can put it, "Fadil, avoid him. He's out of control. I can't handle him any more either. He has strong people in Serbia. Quite simply stay out of his way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we know the timing of this? Because the interpreter didn't catch part of it on line 2 and 3, the interpreter mentions that but also it would be good I think to know when the witness went to see Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me, what was this that was falling on Samac? You said something.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a multiple rocket launcher firing from Croatia, that's what I meant by an abbreviation. It depends but it can fire 32 rockets, 16 rockets, 8 rockets, at the same time, as many as they want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, during this first meeting of the Crisis Staff, when you came there, how would you explain this situation to the Trial Chamber? On the basis of your personal experience. You were talking about Crni and Stiv. At that moment, when you were present, could anybody influence them in any way? How would you describe this to the Trial Chamber? Were they under somebody's control or what was the situation? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to this. I mean, the evidence of the witness is that he turned up and that there was simply discussion. How this particular witness could know who was influencing whom, since he didn't even know the reason he was there and had not -- or he just couldn't tell who was -- who was influencing whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Di Fazio, he was there for quite sometime so for the period he was present he made observations so he can answer. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stiv, Stevan Todorovic, was the man who was doing most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Topcagic was this an official meeting or were there many more people there, how would you describe this? What is your personal knowledge in this regard?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the people who I could remember as being there. I don't even know whether all of them were members of the Crisis Staff. I just know that Miroslav Tadic wasn't then. That's what I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now have Exhibit D55/1, please? Or maybe -- it's time for our break. Maybe, Your Honour, we could deal with this exhibit after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Could we have please, Ms. Registrar, D55/1 please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Topcagic, do you see the name of Dragan Djordjevic, known as Crni, on this list?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the name of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the name of Milan Milicic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, just before the document goes away, do you see your own name on this payroll list of the Crisis Staff for May, 1992, dated 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who drew up this list but I never received any money. It says here, I don't know, it's written in hand, added on later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But whose signature is that? Do you recognise the signature, bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There is a name there, in typing is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, here, oh, down here Mitar Mitrovic, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Topcagic, in your 92 bis statement, in paragraph 39, on page 10, it says as follows: "I brought him to Crkvina straight to the cultural club and helped him go in." Have you found it, Mr. Topcagic, 39?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 39, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on page 10?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please turn to page 10. It's the same paragraph and it continues. And you see this sentence which begins, "There was a room there in which there were some medicines, some bandages and the first aid kit"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You abide by the statement you signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, we've finished with this topic, Mr. Topcagic. We'll move on now. Tell me, please, since you were in Samac during the war, in connection with the role and behaviour of Blagoje Simic, do you have any personal knowledge of him discriminating against the non-Serb population of Samac?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you, Mr. Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a few questions in connection with the responses this witness made to the Prosecutor. Cross-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, my name is Dragan Krgovic on behalf of Mr. Tadic I will put some questions to you on his behalf. Answering to questions put to you by the Prosecutor, you mentioned the shooting at the house of Miroslav Tadic in the early morning hours of the 17th of April. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that, and I abide by that. Shots were fired in the morning on his house from the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a little later, shots were also fired at Miroslav Tadic's house by masked men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Masked men shot at the balcony of his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say masked men, were these the special purpose unit members from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the specials from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are speaking of two instances of shooting at his house, early in the morning when it was the Muslims who fired shots?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the other one a little later when it was the sareni who fired shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Topcagic, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no additional questions for Mr. Topcagic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I just have a few questions for you, Mr. Topcagic. One thing in your statement, in paragraph 11 -- Sorry, my microphone wasn't on, I apologise. I just have a few questions for you, Mr. Topcagic. The first is in your statement in paragraph 11 the first few words, you say the 4th Detachment never existed officially. And I would just like to know what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a typing error here. It never lined up officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Meaning? It never lined up officially? What does that mean? Do you think you could explain?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in Samac did this 4th Detachment line up in a public place when everyone gathers together and stands in a line with their rifles, I don't know how to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist, Your Honour, in our language, there are words "postojati" meaning "existing," and "postrojiti" meaning "lining up." They are very similar and perhaps this is what the witness -- line up. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, might I respectfully suggest that Your Honour invite the witness to read out the transcript of paragraph 11? I've looked at the matter myself and it may assist Your Honour's inquiry to have it read out. If I may respectfully suggest that, to assist Your Honour's line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Topcagic, if you could read paragraph 11 out, it's a fairly short paragraph. Oh, yes, and please if you could read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will read it slowly but with this correction, because I am sure that this, what it says here existed, I'm sure that's not what was meant but lined up. "The 4th Detachment never officially lined up but I know that in it there were companies, platoons and squads. I know that the company squad and platoon leaders were not only Serbs but also Muslims and Croats. I was the leader of the reconnaissance squad. In my squad there were Serbs, Croats and Muslims. The squad numbered 10 men in peace time, or rather in peace time it had no tasks. The reconnaissance squad was under the direct command of the commander, Radovan Antic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for doing that. My second question concerns what you were asked yesterday concerning the collection of weapons by the 4th Detachment and in fact I believe LiveNote yesterday it was page 65, line 17, you answered that Mr. Miroslav Tadic and Mr. Simo Zaric were not present at the time when you were with the other members of the 4th Detachment at the house of Esad Dagovic. I'm sure you recall that from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Sabrija Dagovic's house, and Sulejman Dagovic's house and the house of Jusuf Arnautovic, I guarantee that neither Miroslav Tadic nor Simo Zaric were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So my -- that was just setting my question, just to remind you of what you said yesterday. So my question to you is: You've said they were not there at -- in the yard or the houses of those three families but were they in the vicinity? Were they across the street? Were they perhaps on the corner of Edvard Kardelja Street and Pero Bosic Street?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where we were at that time, they were not there, nor did I see them. They might have been on another part of the street where I couldn't see them, but at that point in time, they were not there at all. I assert that and I guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Third question is: Do you know why Dr. Blagoje Simic was in a room with medical equipment, bandages and so on in Crkvina rather than being in Bosanski Samac? Do you know why there was a small medical facility already set up in Crkvina at the time that you took the wounded man, Debeli, by car there? If you know. If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I saw was the usual first aid kit that every nurse has. As for Mr. Blagoje Simic's presence there, I don't know what his job was there at that moment or his function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Topcagic, I have a couple of questions. Yesterday you told us that the group collecting weapons on the 18th of April consisted of members of the 4th Detachment only. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And the one where you was a member or -- yes, a member of that group, yes. There was -- and you told us yesterday also that there was another group also collecting weapons. You spoke about two groups. Do you by chance remember the composition of that other group?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Do you know a person by name Naser Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Was he taking part in the collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Neither in your group or in the other group?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a policeman in the Samac police station under Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: On the 19th, the following day, did you participate in the collecting of weapons about which you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FADIL TOPCAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, a lot of people brought their weapons on their own initiative, or asked me to come to their houses to take the weapons so that it would not become known that they had had them, because before that, I could not have dreamed that there were so many illegal weapons that the Muslims had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topcagic for giving evidence. We are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, maybe I should first give the redacted version with the assistance of Mr. Usher, of the witness's statement. According to the ruling of the Trial Chamber from March 11, page 16479, there is no examination-in-chief of the witness. There is only -- well, first that was one hour allowed for cross-examination of the Prosecution but after that, the Prosecution actually switched the time for witness -- another witness that was allotted one hour and they have actually 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could just introduce the witness, give his name and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karlovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karlovic, and could you please tell us for the transcript what your name and surname is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Karlovic and my nickname is Kico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your statement has been admitted into evidence and it is the ruling of the Trial Chamber that as such, along with certain amendments or rather redacting certain paragraphs, should become part of the evidence in this case. So I am not going to lead you through any kind of examination. So you will just be examined by the Prosecutor in relation to what happened on the 16th and 17th of April, until the end of the 17th of end in accordance with the decision of the Trial Chamber. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I have understood it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On a point of information or just an issue, this witness has barely given any information on the 16th and 17th. He was home on the 16th. And the 17th he goes off to the SIT factory and then goes to the banks of the river. There are several issues I'd like to raise with him. We only have 20 minutes relating to other days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can cross-examine him according to the areas you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Provided you stick to your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karlovic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Phillip Weiner and I'm going to be asking you some questions this afternoon for a very short period concerning the statement which you provided to this Court. Okay? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I have fully understood you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, you indicated in your statement, in your 92 bis statement that you lived in a part of town called Donji Mahala?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, now I'd like to go back to the early morning hours of the 17th of April in 1992 and you stated that about 2.00, 3.00 in the morning, you heard some shooting, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that some Serbian paramilitaries or volunteers came to your home, they asked who you were, you showed them your identification and that you were a 4th Detachment member, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they told you to stay home, you remained in the house, and eventually, or after a short while, the firing stopped or the sound of the firing stops, and it's quiet.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the morning hours, you go outside and you see your neighbours and you're talking to them, early morning. You didn't indicate the time but I'm assuming around day break, maybe about 6, 7, 8.00, you see your neighbours you're talking to them, it's quiet outside, you're trying to figure out what is happening, what had occurred during the night?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly the way it was. However I would like to say a few words, if possible. That morning, when these paramilitary formations arrived in my part of town, in my street, and sometime around 3.00 exactly, shooting was heard, and I got up and I immediately told my family members that something bad was going on. From the living-room, I went to the sitting room and I saw these people who were in uniform, in many-colour uniforms, they had some kind of caps, black caps, and hats. They were -- they all -- they all had some kind of cream on too. So I could not see anyone properly. I immediately told my son, who was lying in his bedroom, I asked him to come to get up, to see these people and see if he can recognise any of them. He got up, he looked and he said, "Dad, it's not only one man, these are several people who are there, and they are towards the Sava River on the railroad." And this railroad was used for bringing goods to our port, Prestenice. And after a while, these people stayed there for a while, I mean, and it is only natural that they returned to this street, they came to my house, they followed a bullet, they walked up to my door, I felt this. I felt this in the hall of my apartment and at that moment one of them hit my door with a rifle butt. I automatically opened the door. I put my right-hand out and I said that I was surrendering. He told me to go out. I did go out. And then he asked me the following: "Sir, who are you?" I kept silent for a while and then I said that I was a Croat. He used a vulgar expression, he said that he cursed my Croat mother, and he assaulted me but I moved back a step or two. I locked the door but my wife was more aware of what was going on than me. She said open the door because you don't know what can happen. I did, and at that moment my neighbour, Ziko Mlinarevic and Simo also a neighbour of mine, they were all watching this through their doors and their doors were facing my door and they opened the door and they said do not touch him, he is our man. And it is only then that they started reacting. They asked me whether I had any weapons, and who I got them from. I said that I got the weapon from the Yugoslav People's Army and that I'm a member of the 4th Detachment. And I showed them certificates and they told me to go into my house and not to go out for 24 hours. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You have a lot of detail in your statement. I'm just trying to touch upon certain areas of your statement. You don't have to repeat everything that's in your statement, sir. The question I have is: Once again, it's quiet in the morning, you talk to your neighbours, is that about 7, 8.00 in the morning and you're all trying to figure out what's happening?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About 10.00 in the morning, a fewer hours later I assume it's still quiet and you're at home and one of the neighbours comes by with a report -- with a notice that everyone is to report to the SIT building to the 4th Detachment? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. It is correct that we received information, that we were supposed to report at a particular place. But on that day, on the 17th, we were not in that kind of situation. How should I put this? We were not brave enough. We were not brave enough to leave, to travel to the SIT, because in town, there was still a lot of commotion. That was caused by these people who had come to our town. And on that day I and my friends did not go but we went on the 18th. And when we came to the SIT there was no one at the SIT so then we went to the command which had been transferred to sljivak, to the house of Jovo, now Jovo Dusanovic, yes, when I got there, I found a great many of my friends and comrades there and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay before we get to that, let's take it a step at a time. So you didn't go out on the 17th but in Donja Mahala it was --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was still quiet?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, inside the town you had those Serb volunteers in the camouflage uniforms, the one that had come to your house that were in the town part that were scaring people, correct, isn't that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no battling going on street to street in Donja Mahala that morning, it was quiet in Donja Mahala on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There was no battling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on to another portion of your statement. Now, you indicated that in May, there was a large -- I'm sorry, I just want to ask you go this first. In May of 1992, were you aware that a large number of Serbs had been detained or held in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: A large number of Serbs, it was said correctly over radio and television that they were detained in Odzak about 3700 people, I heard that personally with my very own ears from Belgrade television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you also heard over radio Samac, which upset you, that approximately 3700 were killed at the stadium in Odzak, and you were worried about that, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, too. And may I just make another contribution in that respect? May I add something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, because we have very little time, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When I heard that on that day, I was totally taken aback, disappointed, as a man who did not want all of these things to happen, and on that day, Mr. Simo Zaric came to the command at the memorial centre. I met him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that very quickly so we can move through that. You asked Simo about the 3700 Serbs being killed and he told you not to worry, that it's propaganda, isn't that correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And I wouldn't make any further comments in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know that there was no 3700 people killed in Odzak, in fact a lot of those people came to Samac as refugees, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on a little bit later that month, just shortly after these Serbs get arrested or held in Odzak, a large number of Croats are then arrested or held at the high school. You said approximately 150 or so.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was close to the secondary school and the elementary school at the memorial centre Mitar Trifunovic, Uco, at the command I was providing security for the facility and I was watching this. People were indeed being brought in all the time. That's true. And it was my assessment that it was about 150 or 200 people that were moving, how should I put this now, towards this prison or detention centre, yes, detention would be a better word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this high school which became a prison or detention centre was holding approximately 200 Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know and you've indicated that entire families were transferred to Zasavica at the same time. That's what you had heard, entire families were also being transferred to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that. I didn't see it, but I heard that families from the town and most probably from the villages too were taken to the camp in Zasavica where they stayed for a while, and there were a lot of refugees who had fled from other places and who were there together with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who were transported to Zasavica, these entire families that were taken and placed, those were Croats and Muslims, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who were being held at the high school in [as said] Zasavica, did you hear at the time the word in relation to those people being held was they were being isolated or it was some sort of isolation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, maybe just for the -- to have a clear transcript, here it says people who were being held at the high school in Zasavica, this is how it say in the transcript. High school and Zasavica probably because there is no high school in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The high school and in Zasavica, those people were being isolated. Did you hear that term, isolation, or isolated or being isolated, that term or phrase?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that word isolation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, you knew that these people were being isolated because they were Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's move on to September, 1992. You have a discussion with Simo Zaric and you talk about the madness that was going on in Samac. That's your term, the madness, you wanted an end to this madness going on in Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Madness, madness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you refer to madness you were referring to the arrest of the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to the murder of Muslims and Croats at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to the detention and isolation of Muslims and Croats at various facilities in Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to the mistreatment of Muslims and Croats in these detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally you were also referring to the mass looting that was going on in Samac in many homes and businesses especially those of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Not only Croats and Muslims. After 24 hours, when you went out into town, there was not a single shop that was intact. Everything had been looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were referring to the mass looting too. Now, this madness that you were referring to all started after April 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it began with the takeover of the town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it began with the establishment of a Serbian municipality which was controlled by a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But sir, let's go to the summer, actually the spring of 1992 and the summer of 1992. And let's talk about, let's get a little bit more detail about the government. The civilian government. You knew that the police, the Crisis Staff, or later the War Presidency, and the military, during those months, the spring and summer, took no action to have Lugar arrested for the Crkvina massacre?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Unless there is a basis for this question, whether he knew or not, and then ask him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like me to respond on the basis or just ask the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that the civilian authorities, meaning the police, the Crisis Staff, as well as the military, took no action to arrest Lugar and those other paramilitaries for the massacre of Muslims and Croat civilians at Crkvina, you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that but I heard two or three days later that what had been done with these 16 people was done and they were killed by Lugar but who issued the order, I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question is you new that no one took any action to arrest Lugar and arrest the others for committing those crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In the memorial centre, I heard that a young soldier had been killed who had been in the fighting and he had been there with Lugar. So Lugar was very upset by this and wanted revenge and then he went to Crkvina and did what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you -- everyone in town was talking about this incident, the massacre of civilians at Crkvina. However, no one ever said Lugar was arrested, you knew that Lugar was walking around town and that the police, the Crisis Staff and the military never took any action to see that Lugar was arrested for this terrible act. No one did anything, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct that nobody did anything but as far as I heard what this man was like, believe it or not, everybody was afraid of him, the military, civilians, all of us who were there, if we came close to him, we would move away because we didn't want to run into such a man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you never heard the Crisis Staff call for a day of mourning or even make a public statement indicating how sad it was about what had happened at Crkvina. They didn't do that either, did they? Not even issue a public statement.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nothing was announced in public, there was no public statement, and there was no mourning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also knew that the police, the Crisis Staff, the military, took no action to end the isolation of those non-Serbs that were being held, other than exchanging them outside of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were exchanges and people were exchanged on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the Crisis Staff, the police, the military, did not take any action to end the isolation of prisoners. You knew that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. I don't know whether they did anything or not. I only know that exchanges were carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not hear of any action being taken by the police, the Crisis Staff or the military to end the isolation of non-Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. I didn't know anything about it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nor did you hear anything about the Crisis Staff, the police or the military doing anything to end the looting in the town. That's why you and Simo Zaric were discussing it in September. They didn't do anything through the spring or summer of 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the Army of Republika Srpska and the 4th Detachment, these men were on the front lines and they didn't have the time or whatever to take any action. There was the police to create order or disorder in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But sir you didn't hear any group doing anything to end the looting, the Crisis Staff, the police, nor the army, no one took any action, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, you mentioned that -- you mentioned that there was an exchange process in the town. Now, you've --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've known Simo Zaric for a very long time, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I've known Simo Zaric for more than 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you trust his word, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I trusted everything and everything was true that I said in my statements and all the people who have come here and sat at this desk to say what they think about Mr. Simo Zaric, I think these are real men who came here to say that he was one of the people who did not want all the things that were happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, Simo Zaric gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 2nd, 1998. We refer to it as P141 which is our exhibit number. And he said as part of this exchange process, the non-Serbs had no choice but to leave Samac. Basically they were forced to leave. Do you agree with Simo Zaric's statement? That's what he said about the exchange system, the non-Serbs of Bosanski Samac had no choice but to leave. Do you agree with Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I didn't understand your question quite well. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When being interviewed by investigators, Simo Zaric said about the exchange system in Samac that the non-Serbs, basically the Muslims and the Croats, had no choice but to leave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with Simo Zaric's statement that the non-Serbs had no choice or were forced to leave Samac? Do you agree with Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with this statement made by Mr. Simo Zaric and I can support it with arguments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wish to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions to ask about the issue of madness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can go ahead with your questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karlovic, I am Mr. Pantelic, Defence counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic. I have only a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked about the competences of the civilian authorities, the army and the police in connection with the events in Samac so please tell me briefly, Mr. Karlovic, what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I am a machinist. I'm a highly skilled mechanic -- mechanist, machinist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a secondary education?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a secondary education but as I'm highly skilled, I'm a little bit higher up than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course you are not a military expert?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not a legal expert?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I'm quite familiar with those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also not a police expert?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how come that you're familiar with these areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you, I spent my entire childhood trying to do something for the common good and I was appointed to all kinds of positions in the former Yugoslavia. I was even a member of the central committee of the League of Communists of Bosnia and Herzegovina and vice-president of the assembly in the municipal assembly in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also a member of the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a member of the League of Social Democrats led by Mr. Dodik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, you were a member of what party?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not belong to any party, because my party at that time was in the opposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What party was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The Socialist Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about some sort of madness.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of the massacre of Serbs in Sijekovac in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. It's the madness we are talking about in Bosanski Samac and that's exactly what he said in his statement, Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's related to the issue of madness. I just want to clarify what is the meaning of madness for this witness, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Mr. Pantelic, you know very well you've read the statement of this witness. So you're question is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether it was your understanding that the establishment of the Serbian Municipality of Samac and the Crisis Staff led to madness in Samac. You remember the question and your answer, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the madness started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer the question. Please, we don't have much time. So stick to the question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the madness started on the 16th and 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please wait a little. On the basis of your personal experience and knowledge, how would you describe the political events in Samac and the relationship between the SDA and the HDZ against the SDS? Do you know anything about this in person? Would you describe this as madness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... has to concern issues prior to April 17th. I only discussed from April 17th on. That's outside the scope. He's trying to get into the whole history from January through April of the disagreements between the HDZ, the SDA and the SDS. And that's totally outside the scope of any cross-examination that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, Mr. Weiner is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karlovic, please, are you aware of the fact that Lugar was arrested twice, once in July and once in December, 1992, when he was also tried before the military court in Banja Luka? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the following, that in autumn, 1992, in Samac, there were no more detainees or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that during 1992, and 1993, about 10.000 Serb refugees came to Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour, for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It will not take more than a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm asking for the patience of the interpreters. Maybe we can conclude this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karlovic, due to the fact that time has been very limited, some things got into the transcript in great haste but I wanted to save time and clarify this at the very end. When you said that you were on guard in front of the command of the 4th Detachment --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since it wasn't very clear in the transcript, I mean the way it turned out, you stood guard in front of the 4th Detachment, not in front of the elementary and secondary school?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In response to the Prosecutor's questions, you said what the situation was like in Donja Mahala in your neighbourhood where you lived and where you still live. From the 17th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not experience any combat there. I remember that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one more thing, sir. In relation to certain events. Do you know, do you know about the fact that on the 17th of April, 1992, two of your fellow citizens were killed, Dzebic, Ivica and Lukic, Ilija, who worked in the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know that. That was the morning when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the checkpoint by the public security station, a certain Ilija Vuckovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is your conclusion in respect of this? Was there any fighting or was there not any fighting since these people got killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these people killed without any fighting. This Ilija, he was going from work, he was a bit deaf, and they shouted stop and he did not stop and it's only natural that they did what they did. As far as this little Dzebic was concerned, he was at a hotel, he was a waiter, he came home about 4.00. He went into his house, he undressed, he went to bed, and then a raid began and he had quite a bit of this money, this Croatian money, that's probably what they saw, that's what I heard about it at any rate, he resisted a bit, and they killed him on the spot in his own kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karlovic, you are finished with your evidence. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, the interpreters and supporting staff. We have now reached the end of our session. We will continue our proceedings on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 1.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
